text: How Snow Gums Survive a Bushfire. Snow gums grow high in the mountains, where summer bushfires can sweep through the trees. A strong fire can kill every leaf and branch on a snow gum, but the tree is not finished. Hidden at the base of its trunk is a woody lump called a lignotuber. This lump stores food, and it is covered in sleeping buds. Because the lump is partly underground, the soil protects it from the heat of the flames. After the fire has passed, the burnt tree can no longer make food in its leaves. This change wakes the sleeping buds. They use the food stored in the lump to send up new green shoots. Within a few years, the shoots grow into a ring of new stems around the old, dead trunk. That is why many snow gums have several thin trunks instead of one thick one.

text: How a Guitar Makes Its Sound. When you pluck a guitar string, it moves backwards and forwards very quickly. This is called vibrating. A thick string vibrates more slowly than a thin one, so it makes a lower note. The vibrating string pushes on the air around it and makes tiny waves. On its own, a string is quite quiet, because it is too thin to move much air. That is why a guitar has a hollow wooden body. The string passes its shaking through the bridge into the thin wooden top of the guitar. The whole top starts to vibrate, and because it is much bigger than the string, it pushes far more air. The air inside the body bounces around and comes out of the round sound hole. By the time the sound reaches your ears, it is many times louder than the string alone. That is why you can hear a guitar from the back of a hall, even though its strings are thinner than spaghetti.

frame: Tully is reading up before the Architect's space camp. The Whyrella is reading over her shoulder.
text: Why Astronauts' Bones Get Weaker in Space. On Earth, your skeleton works hard every second of the day, even when you are just standing in line at the canteen. Gravity pulls your body towards the ground, so your bones must hold up your weight with every step. This constant load sends a signal to special cells inside your bones, telling them to keep building fresh, strong bone. On a space station, however, astronauts float, so their legs, hips and spine have almost no weight to carry. Without that load, the bone-building cells receive no signal and slow down, while other cells keep breaking old bone down at the usual rate. As a result, an astronaut can lose around one per cent of the bone in their hips and legs every month. The lost minerals travel into the blood, which is also why some astronauts develop painful kidney stones. Exercise machines that make astronauts push against heavy springs can slow this loss, because they create some of the load that gravity normally provides. Astronauts also eat foods rich in calcium and vitamin D, which their bodies need to build new bone. Even so, after returning to Earth, it can take years for their bones to fully recover.

text: How a Compass Finds North. Deep inside the Earth, a core of hot, liquid iron is constantly churning, and this movement turns the whole planet into a gigantic, weak magnet. Like any magnet, the Earth has two magnetic poles, one near the North Pole and one near the South Pole, and invisible lines of magnetic force loop between them. Scientists call the space around a magnet, where its pull can be felt, a magnetic field. A compass needle is a thin sliver of magnetised metal, balanced on a pin so that it can spin with almost no friction. Because the needle is a tiny magnet itself, its ends are pulled by the Earth's magnetic field, and the needle swings until it lines up with those invisible lines. The end marked in red is attracted towards the magnetic pole in the north, which is why it always settles pointing that way. However, the magnetic pole is not in exactly the same place as the North Pole on a map, and it slowly wanders over the years. Near the far north of Canada, the gap between the two can be so large that a compass is almost useless. That is why a compass and a map can disagree by a few degrees.
